title: Chapter 3.  History — The French Colonial Period

blocks.content: This is Puducherry's most distinctive and heavily tested history chapter: as a French colonial possession for close to three centuries, Puducherry (along with Karaikal, Mahe, Yanam and Chandernagore in Bengal) forms the core of India's 'French India' (Etablissements francais dans l'Inde) - a colonial history entirely separate from, and often confused with, British India's much more extensively studied history.

The French East India Company (Compagnie francaise des Indes orientales, chartered in 1664 under Louis XIV's minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert) established its first settlement in India relatively later than the Portuguese, Dutch and British, with Francois Martin founding Pondicherry (Puducherry) as a French trading post in 1673, acquiring the site from the local Sultan of Bijapur/Golconda-era authority.

Francois Martin is regarded as the effective founder and first major administrator of French Pondicherry, developing it from a small fishing settlement into a fortified, planned colonial town over subsequent decades, laying the groundwork for the town's distinctive grid-planned 'White Town' (Chapter 1) still visible today.

The French subsequently established or acquired the other constituent territories of French India at various points: Chandernagore (in Bengal, acquired 1673, now part of West Bengal rather than the Puducherry UT), Karaikal (acquired 1739 from the Nawab of Arcot/Thanjavur ruler), Mahe (acquired 1721-25, on the Malabar Coast), and Yanam (acquired 1723, on the Godavari delta).

cells: West Bengal (NOT part of the present Puducherry UT - merged into West Bengal in 1954-55, distinct from the 1962/1963 process covered in Chapter 4)

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Chandernagore was ALSO a French colonial possession (like the four territories of present-day Puducherry UT) but is NOT part of the Puducherry UT today - it was merged into West Bengal following a SEPARATE, earlier 1949-1955 process, distinct from the 1954/1962-63 transfer covered for the other four territories in Chapter 4. This is a very frequently tested distinguishing fact.

Pondicherry's history through the 18th century was dominated by intense Anglo-French colonial and commercial rivalry, playing out through the three Carnatic Wars (fought in southern India between roughly 1746 and 1763), which mirrored and were connected to the wider European conflicts of the period (the War of the Austrian Succession and the Seven Years' War).

Joseph Francois Dupleix, French Governor-General of Pondicherry from 1742, is the single most significant figure of this period - an ambitious administrator who pursued an expansionist policy of alliance-building with local Indian rulers and direct military intervention in regional succession disputes, briefly making French power in southern India appear ascendant over the rival British East India Company.

Despite early French successes (including the capture of Madras from the British in 1746 during the First Carnatic War), the wider Anglo-French struggle in India ultimately favoured the British: Dupleix was recalled to France in 1754 amid the French Company's financial strain and dissatisfaction with the costly ongoing conflict, and Pondicherry itself was captured and its fortifications destroyed by British forces in 1761, at the height of the Seven Years' War.

Pondicherry was restored to France by the Treaty of Paris (1763), which ended the Seven Years' War, though the French were permitted only to maintain trading rights, not to refortify their possessions or maintain a significant military presence, considerably diminishing France's subsequent colonial ambitions in India compared to the earlier Dupleix era.

cells: Joseph Francois Dupleix becomes Governor-General of Pondicherry
Pondicherry captured and fortifications destroyed by the British (Seven Years' War)
Treaty of Paris restores Pondicherry to France (with restricted military/fortification rights)

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Dupleix's recall to France (1754) PREDATES Pondicherry's actual capture by the British (1761) by seven years - a frequently tested sequencing fact showing that French decline in India was already underway administratively before the final military defeat.
Later French Rule & Repeated British Occupations

Following the 1763 Treaty of Paris, Pondicherry and the other French settlements continued under nominal French sovereignty but were repeatedly occupied by the British during subsequent Anglo-French conflicts of the late 18th and early 19th centuries (including periods during the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars), before being finally and permanently restored to France after the Napoleonic Wars concluded in 1815, remaining under continuous French administration from 1816 until India's independence-era transfer process (Chapter 4).

Through the 19th and early 20th centuries, French India (the five settlements collectively) developed its own distinct administrative, legal and cultural character, including French-language education, a French-influenced legal and civic administrative system, and, notably, extending French citizenship rights to Indian residents of the territories under specified conditions - a stark contrast to British India's more restrictive approach to extending metropolitan citizenship to colonial subjects.

★ EXAM POINT: French India's settlements were finally, permanently restored to France in 1816 (after the Napoleonic Wars) - remaining under continuous French rule for well over a century afterward, right up to the mid-20th-century transfer process. This 1763-vs-1816 distinction (temporary restoration vs. final, lasting restoration) is a frequently tested nuance.

items: French East India Company (chartered 1664); Francois Martin founded Pondicherry in 1673.
French India = Pondicherry (1673), Chandernagore (1673, now in West Bengal), Yanam (1723), Mahe (1721-25), Karaikal (1739).
Joseph Francois Dupleix (Governor-General from 1742) was the key figure of French ascendancy; recalled 1754.
Pondicherry captured by the British in 1761 (Seven Years' War); restored to France by the Treaty of Paris, 1763 (with restricted fortification rights).
Pondicherry finally, permanently restored to France in 1816, after the Napoleonic Wars - remained under continuous French rule until the mid-20th-century transfer process (Chapter 4).
